progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: see Scope. Students have watched bio-m6-b05, bio-m6-b18, bio-m5-b09 and bio-m8-b06.
progression.startsWith: A couple of days after birth, nearly every baby born in NSW is offered a heel-prick blood test, checking for more than twenty conditions. One of them, PKU, can cause severe brain damage, yet babies found this way can grow up without it. So did the test prevent a genetic disease, or only find it? That's today's question: when can genetics help prevent disease?
progression.stopsAfter: naming the three jobs of genetic technology (screening finds, embryo testing chooses, engineering changes) and the three things "prevent" can mean; explaining how newborn screening and a low-phenylalanine diet prevent PKU's brain damage while the alleles stay unchanged and heritable, and why screening helps only when an early treatment exists; explaining carriers, the one in four risk for two carriers of a recessive condition, carrier screening and non-directive counselling; explaining PGT (IVF, cells from the outer layer at about day five, test for the known variant, transfer an unaffected embryo) as selection, not engineering, with its limits; explaining somatic gene therapy (a viral vector delivering a working gene; a CRISPR edit of a patient's own blood stem cells) as treatment of one person that does not change inheritance; explaining why germline editing is prohibited in Australia; giving biological, practical and access limits (multifactorial disease, variants of uncertain significance, cost) and the main ethical questions; applying this to an SMA carrier couple and to Huntington's disease.
progression.nextLesson: bio-m8-b15, how technology assists a disorder that is already present: hearing loss.

teaching.task: A heel-prick test lets babies with PKU grow up without brain damage. Did the test prevent a genetic disease, or only find it? When can genetics help prevent disease?
teaching.causalExplanation: Genetic technologies do three different jobs. Screening finds a risk or a condition, but it doesn't change any DNA. Embryo testing chooses between embryos that already exist. Genetic engineering changes the genetic material itself. So for any method, ask which job it does, and what exactly it prevents: symptoms in a person, the birth of an affected child, or the faulty gene itself. Start with the heel prick. In PKU, short for phenylketonuria, both copies of one gene are faulty, so the liver makes too little working enzyme to break down phenylalanine, an amino acid in ordinary protein. Phenylalanine builds up in the blood and damages the developing brain. If the test finds it early, the baby starts a low-phenylalanine diet straightaway, the level stays low, and the brain develops normally. The faulty alleles are still there in every cell, and they can still be passed on. What the diet prevents is the harmful phenotype, the effect the genes have on the body, because it limits the phenylalanine the weak pathway can't handle. That's why screening only helps when there's something useful to do next. A test for a condition nothing can treat finds it, but it doesn't prevent it.
teaching.conversationalApproach: A couple of days after birth, nearly every baby born in NSW is offered a heel-prick blood test, checking for more than twenty conditions. Genetic technologies do three different jobs. Start with the heel prick. The faulty alleles are still there in every cell, and they can still be passed on. The second job is finding risk before a pregnancy. A genetic counsellor explains the options without steering the couple's choice. The third job is changing genes. Editing an egg, sperm or early embryo is called germline editing. So why can't genetics prevent most disease? The biggest limit is biology. There are ethical questions too. Two exam questions. One in four, because each carrier passes on the variant half the time. Second. Screening only prevents symptoms when an early treatment exists, like the diet for PKU. So for any genetic prevention question, name the job: find, choose or change.
teaching.openingDecision: A couple of days after birth, nearly every baby born in NSW is offered a heel-prick blood test, checking for more than twenty conditions. One of them, PKU, can cause severe brain damage, yet babies found this way can grow up without it. So did the test prevent a genetic disease, or only find it? That's today's question: when can genetics help prevent disease?
teaching.understandingCheck: Two exam questions. First. Carrier screening shows that both members of a couple carry a variant for spinal muscular atrophy, an autosomal recessive condition. State the chance that each pregnancy is affected. Then explain how PGT could reduce the chance of an affected child, and why it isn't genetic engineering. Pause here to answer. Second. Huntington's disease is caused by one dominant allele, and symptoms usually begin in adulthood. No current treatment prevents them. Explain why newborn screening would not prevent Huntington's disease. Then assess one genetic technology that could reduce its effect on a family. Pause here to answer.
teaching.curriculumScope: B8-IQ4-01: "use secondary sources to evaluate the effectiveness of current disease-prevention methods and develop strategies for the prevention of a non-infectious disease, including but not limited to:" with the listed example "genetic engineering". Evaluate effectiveness: scenes 4, 6 to 10 and attempt 2. Develop a strategy: attempt 1 (b) and the decision rule. Inquiry question: "How can non-infectious diseases be prevented?"

design.visualSystem: One three-jobs bar sits along the top of the frame from scene 2 to scene 10: three coded tabs, "find" (magnifier outline), "choose" (a tick between two embryo outlines), "change" (a small edit mark on a DNA strand); the current job lights and the others dim. Under it, a "what's prevented?" strip at the bottom from scene 2: three slots, "symptoms", "an affected birth", "the gene itself", one of which lights green for each method (PKU lights "symptoms"; PGT lights "an affected birth"; somatic therapy lights a grey "symptoms, in one person"; germline would light "the gene itself" but carries a red "prohibited in Australia" tag). Above, one painted plate or matched pair at a time with callouts. No people: couples appear only as two coded allele chips ("carrier", "carrier"); the baby only as the blood-spot card. At most three bright text items at once; earlier labels dim to grey.
design.transitionPlan: no people. the card shrinks to the upper left. the "find" tab lights. the two amber allele chips stay bright and a grey tag reads "genotype unchanged, still heritable"; a small coded arrow carries one chip down to a "next generation" slot. the "find" tab stays lit. on "genetic counsellor" a coded panel lists three option chips with equal weight and no arrow pointing at any: "use PGT", "test during pregnancy", "no testing" (grey tag "non-directive: information, not instructions"). the "change" tab lights. the blastocyst plate returns small with a coded edit mark on its inner cells; on "germline" a coded arrow runs from the embryo to a small egg-and-sperm chip (label "germline"), and on "be inherited" a dashed arrow carries the mark to a coded three-generation row of plain circles (label "can be inherited"; grey tag "not every cell is always edited"). the jobs bar dims. a coded balance draws (abstract, no people). the board clears. the card stays. the board clears. the card stays. the JobsBar returns at the centre with "find, choose, change" hand-lettered beneath; the PreventedStrip sits below it; three small limit chips write in a row: "biology", "access", "ethics". > Here are the key notes.

scenes.visualReference: on "genetic counsellor" a coded panel lists three option chips with equal weight and no arrow pointing at any: "use PGT", "test during pregnancy", "no testing" (grey tag "non-directive: information, not instructions"). On "PGT" the "choose" tab lights and the gloss writes "PGT: preimplantation genetic testing". m6-egg-sperm-dish-v1.png enters small (grey tag "IVF"). On "about five days" the dish gives way to new m8-blastocyst-v1.png large (grey tag "day 5 embryo"); on "outer layer" a callout traces the outer cell layer (label "outer layer → placenta"; grey tag "trophectoderm") and a second callout marks the inner cluster (label "inner cells → baby"). On "A few cells are taken" the matched state m8-blastocyst-biopsy-v1.png cross-fades in (same embryo with a fine glass pipette at the outer layer holding a few cells). On "tested for the family's known variant" a row of five small blastocyst thumbnails (the same plate, repeated, small) appears with coded result chips under each: three amber "variant", two green "unaffected". On "Only an unaffected embryo is transferred" one green embryo lifts slightly; the others dim. Through the biopsy, testing and selection the source embryo (biopsy state, small, upper left) and its few extracted outer cells stay visible, joined to the thumbnail row by a thin coded line, so the tested cells are always traceable to their embryo. On "no embryo's DNA is changed" a small SlimStrand under each embryo stays unedited and the "change" tab flashes grey with a small "not this" tag; hand-lettered "selection" writes under the "choose" tab. The narration pauses 1 s after "changed" (an edit-time gap in the voiced take, not a re-recorded line) so the unedited strands can be read. The PreventedStrip lights "an affected birth" green. On the limits two grey chips write beside the embryos, "variant must be known" and "IVF: cost, burden" (grey tag "few embryos, may all be affected"). A grey tag in the corner: "testing during pregnancy (NIPT, amniocentesis): not covered here". Earlier chips dim so at most three items are bright. Hold one second.

scenes.motionPurpose: the blastocyst plate returns small with a coded edit mark on its inner cells; on "germline" a coded arrow runs from the embryo to a small egg-and-sperm chip (label "germline"), and on "be inherited" a dashed arrow carries the mark to a coded three-generation row of plain circles (label "can be inherited"; grey tag "not every cell is always edited"). The pathway stays visible to the end of the scene. On "passed to children" the PreventedStrip's "the gene itself" slot outlines, and the scene 7 thumbnail "symptoms, in one person" sits beside it in grey for the contrast, then takes a red tag "prohibited in Australia" (grey tag "Prohibition of Human Cloning for Reproduction Act 2002"). On each reason a chip writes: "no consent possible", "wrong edits inherited", "can't be reversed". At most three bright items. Hold one second.

Hold one second.

scenes.visualReference: the board clears. The card writes on, tagged "HSC-style question, written for HSCScience". Stem: "Carrier screening shows that both members of a couple carry a variant for spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), an autosomal recessive condition." Demand: "(a) State the chance that each pregnancy is affected. (1 mark) (b) Explain how preimplantation genetic testing (PGT) could reduce the chance of an affected child, and why it is not genetic engineering. (3 marks)". No plate and no people. The countdown ring starts after "Pause here to answer." and runs for 10 seconds. The whole card stays on screen during the countdown and after it.

scenes.visualReference: the card stays. On "One in four" "both members ... carry" and "autosomal recessive" underline; a letters-only Punnett grid draws small beside the card (parents "Aa" × "Aa"; offspring AA, Aa, Aa, aa, with "aa" circled; grey tag "a = SMA variant"). Answer (a) writes: "1 in 4 (25%) each pregnancy". On "tested for that known variant" answer (b) builds on the cues: "IVF embryos tested for the known SMA variant", "only an unaffected embryo transferred", "no DNA altered → selection". On "classic mistake" a chip "PGT removes the faulty gene" writes and takes a scribble cross, small text "it chooses; it doesn't change". Settle one second.
scenes.teachingReason: One in four, because each carrier passes on the variant half the time.

scenes.visualReference: the board clears. The card writes on, tagged "HSC-style question, written for HSCScience". Stem: "Huntington's disease is caused by a single dominant allele. Symptoms usually begin in adulthood, and no current treatment prevents them." Demand: "(a) Explain why newborn screening would not prevent Huntington's disease. (2 marks) (b) Assess one genetic technology that could reduce the effect of Huntington's disease on a family. (3 marks)". The countdown ring starts after "Pause here to answer." and runs for 10 seconds. The whole card stays on screen during the countdown and after it.

scenes.visualReference: the card stays. On "an early treatment exists" "no current treatment prevents them" underlines; the scene 4 chain "find early" → "treatment that works early" returns small with the second box empty. Answer (a) writes: "screening needs an early treatment to prevent symptoms; none exists → found, not prevented". On "select embryos without the known allele" "single dominant allele" underlines; answer (b) builds: "PGT: select embryos without the allele → prevents an affected birth", "limits: IVF, cost, ethics", "judgement: useful for some families, not a general prevention". The PreventedStrip returns small with "an affected birth" green. On "classic mistake" a chip "gene therapy can now cure Huntington's" writes and takes a scribble cross, small text "not currently". Settle one second.
scenes.teachingReason: Screening only prevents symptoms when an early treatment exists, like the diet for PKU.
